contribStatement.content: An organised analytical treatment of how recursive computation is modelled and evaluated.

contribDetail.content: The study brings recurrence relations, recursion trees, substitution, asymptotic notation, time and space analysis, applications and practical trade-offs into one coherent account. It is a descriptive, analytical and literature-based study rather than an experimental benchmark.

conclusion.content: Recursive algorithms should be evaluated on both correctness and resource efficiency, and asymptotic analysis provides the common language for that comparison.

conclusionDetail.content: Even when two methods solve the same problem, they can differ significantly in time, auxiliary space, simplicity and behaviour on particular inputs. Understanding these trade-offs is essential for designing scalable software.

signoff.content: Mathematical Analysis of Recursive Algorithms · Department of Data Science · A.Y. 2026–2027

rows.question: What did you learn from this project?
rows.answer: How recursive structure becomes a recurrence, how that recurrence yields an asymptotic bound, and why time and space must always be judged together.

rows.question: What can be done in future?
rows.answer: Implement the discussed methods, benchmark them empirically on larger inputs, visualise recursion trees and call stacks, compare alternative implementations, and study average-case behaviour on real datasets.

rows.label: Recursive algorithms reduce a problem to smaller instances of the same problem, bounded by a base case.
A recurrence such as T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) expresses the cost of recursive computation mathematically.
Recursion trees, substitution and standard results give concrete ways to derive asymptotic bounds.
O, Ω and Θ describe growth independently of processor, language or compiler.
Recursion depth itself consumes auxiliary memory, so time and space are judged together.
Asymptotic analysis is a reliable first framework for scalability, not a prediction of exact runtime.
